claims.text: The baseline eutectic high-entropy alloy contains dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The chemically unmodified internal boundaries are prone to microcracking during tensile deformation.
A minor addition of a ductility-promoting element such as Nb will segregate at lamellar-colony or interphase boundaries.
Controlled dopant addition can promote interfacial segregation without altering the overall eutectic lamellar structure.
Keeping the elemental addition below a critical level will avoid unwanted secondary phases.
Solute segregation will chemically modify and strengthen the relevant interfacial regions.
The segregated element will reduce localized stress concentrations.
The segregated element will improve cohesion at phase boundaries.
Improved phase-boundary cohesion will hinder crack initiation.
The interfacial modification will impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion will increase yield strength.
The interfacial modification will foster more uniform plastic deformation.
More uniform plastic deformation will enhance tensile ductility.
The doped alloy will have higher room-temperature tensile strength than the unmodified baseline.
The doped alloy will have greater room-temperature elongation to fracture than the unmodified baseline.
The beneficial effects will occur only within a narrow dopant-composition window.
Excessive doping or unsuitable processing may cause detrimental phase transformations or lamellar coarsening.
Excessive doping or unsuitable processing may eliminate the improvement or worsen brittleness.

contradictions.description: The target interface is identified inconsistently as lamellar-colony boundaries, interphase boundaries, interfaces between lamellar colonies, and phase boundaries. These are not necessarily the same physical boundary population, leaving the intervention target and proposed mediator ambiguous.
